newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Major steps up election camapign.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major steps up election camapign.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major on Saturday coupled an attack on the main opposition Labour Party with the announcement of new measures to raise standards in Britain's schools.
At a pre-election rally of 2,500 of his Conservative Party's activists, Major likened Labour leader Tony Blair to a travelling salesman who will say and do anything to curry favour.
Major's speech was intended to move the election campign up a gear, aides said.
"New Labour is one great marketing scam. They only say what they are told the customer would like to hear. The exact characteristic of the foot-in-the-door salesman.
"Nothing is quite what it seems. It depends on who they're speaking to," the prime minister said.

Major, who must call an election by May 22, is fighting to claw back Labour's big lead in opinion polls of nearly 20 percentage points. Based on their own surveys, Conservative strategists believe one of their best lines of attack will be to focus on Blair's perceived willingness to be all things to all men.
"They're prepared to disregard the views of a lifetime in the briefing of a lunchtime.
"As day succeeds day, the fraud that is New Labour becomes more transparent. You can't take at face value a word that Labour say. That's why they're so dangerous," Major said.
Labour deputy leader John Prescott, also on the campaign trial in Birmingham, accused Major of being "two-faced".
"When the prime minister promises something you know he will break his word. It doesn't matter what John Major says today -- his past record is clear.
"The two faces of John Major, saying one thing and doing another, betray the trust of the people today, just as he did five years ago," Prescott said.
With education shaping up as a key electoral battleground, Major said the ruling party's manifesto would promise parents a "Guarantee of Standards".
The way national school tests are marked would also be changed so that parents could judge more easily how well their children were doing at ages seven, 11 and 14.
In another move to force up standards, schoool inspectors would be given new powers to take over failing local education authorities -- many of them in Labour hands, Major said.
Major wants to soldier on in power until May in the hope that Britain's strong economy will revive his party's popularity.
But he is operating without a majority in parliament and will be forced into a minority if Labour wins a by-election next Thursday for the seat of Wirral South in northwest England.
Opinion polls suggest Labour will win that vote.
